X.fix: Apply settings on the client or at the origin and never forward them to third parties. Strip `X-Reader-Prefs` before analytics, ban segmenting or storing it by contract, remove the "Accessibility: ..." segments and delete existing ones. If any processing remains, run a DPIA, disclose it on the panel and privacy notice, get separate explicit consent, and do not send IP address or user agent.
X.impact: Settings chosen to make reading possible are used to infer a disability, which is health data (special category under UK GDPR, Article 9). The inference is tied to IP address and user agent, so the person is identifiable, and it is shared with a vendor without visible notice or lawful basis. Disabled readers must give up privacy to get access, and many will stop using the settings.
X.problem: The `rp` cookie becomes `X-Reader-Prefs: size=200;contrast=high;motion=reduce;font=dyslexia;spacing=2;level=simplified;sr=1` and is forwarded "with the reader's IP address and user agent, to the library origin and to Lumen Edge analytics". Analytics builds "reader segments" such as "Accessibility: low vision" and "Accessibility: cognitive", which the library can view. `sr=1` says the person uses a screen reader. The panel says only that settings are saved to the library account and follow the reader to any device, with no mention of a third party, analytics, profiling or IP address.

X.fix: Remove the content-stripping. Use `alt=""` for decorative images, keep footnotes as linked `<aside>`/`role="doc-footnote"` or endnote content, and use landmarks so users can skip asides. Any "simplified layout" option must not depend on disclosing assistive technology, must say exactly what it hides, must collapse rather than delete, and must offer a one-click return to full content.
X.impact: These readers receive a different, incomplete book with no indication of what was removed, so citations, corrections, translators' notes and figure content are lost. Informative images lose their text alternative and structure is lost. It is the discredited separate screen-reader-version pattern; users can already skip clutter with headings and landmarks. Sighted dyslexic text-to-speech users who tick the box are also affected.
X.problem: When `sr=1`, Lumen Edge "removes images and 'decorative' sidebars, including footnotes and the publisher's notes, to 'reduce clutter for screen reader users'". The label says only "I use a screen reader" and does not mention removal. Footnotes and notes are content, not decoration; images can carry information (diagrams, maps, illustrations) and their alt text is removed with them.
X.where: settings.html, "Screen reader mode" fieldset (`<input type="checkbox" name="sr" value="1"> I use a screen reader`); integration.md bullet 3

X.fix: Do not replace text silently. Show a persistent, programmatically exposed banner on each rewritten chapter (for example "Simplified by a computer program. It may contain mistakes. [Show original]"), offer an original/simplified toggle per chapter or paragraph, reword the settings label to say it is machine-rewritten, possibly inaccurate, with the original one click away, get the publisher's agreement, and prefer human-written or human-checked Easy Read editions.
X.impact: Readers with cognitive or learning disabilities, low literacy or a second language, who are least able to spot distortion, may take machine output for the author's words. Facts, meaning, tone and plot can change unnoticed; readers may quote, study or be examined on it. With no marker, a reader who forgot the setting or a person sharing the device cannot tell what they are reading. Best practice is a supplementary version beside the original, not a silent replacement.
X.problem: When `level=simplified`, Lumen Edge "sends the book chapter to its own rewriting model and returns the rewritten chapter. The original publisher is not told, and the rewritten text carries no marker." The label does not say a machine model does the rewriting, that it may be inaccurate or omit things, or that it applies to every book on all devices.
X.where: settings.html, "Reading level" fieldset (`Simplified text (rewritten for easier reading)`); integration.md bullet 2

X.fix: Wrap the save in `try { const r = await fetch(...); if (!r.ok) throw ... }`. On failure write a clear error to the status region (for example "Your settings were not saved. Check your connection and try again.") or use `role="alert"`. Clear the region before writing so repeats are announced. Disable the button with a visible, announced "Saving..." state. Set the cookie only after server confirmation.
X.impact: Users are told settings were saved when they were not, then open a book without the large text, high contrast or reduced motion they need and do not know why. This is silent failure, and hurts screen reader users and people with cognitive disabilities who trust the confirmation.
X.problem: The response is never checked (no `res.ok` test) and there is no `try/catch`. A 4xx or 5xx response still shows "Settings saved.". A network error rejects the promise, so nothing is announced and the button gives no feedback. Nothing marks the save as in progress, and a second save puts identical text into `role="status"`, which many screen readers do not announce again.
